# Habituation {#sec-habituation}

[Getting used to what is always there]{.lb-subtitle}

<div data-life="status" data-stage="1.2h"></div>

::: {.lb-takeaway}
**New:** no new cells. The eyes get used to what they keep seeing: what stays in view fades.

**Result:** the animals stop biting at bushes that never give anything, and spend far less of their life standing
still. Switching the adaptation off costs them more than half their fitness.
:::

The animals of the previous stage respond to a look in the same way every time they see it. An emptied bush still
looks enough like food, so an animal can stand in front of it for a long time, biting. An animal should stop
responding to something that stays the same and keeps giving nothing.

This stage changes one thing, in the eyes: they get used to what they keep seeing. To make that worth having, the
world gets a *dud*, a bush that looks like food and never carries a berry.

<div data-life="brain" data-stage="1.2h"></div>

## The circuit

No new cells. Each of the eyes' **look** inputs keeps a slow average of what it has seen over roughly the last
fifty ticks, and passes on only the **difference** between what it sees now and that average.

Every neuron downstream of the eyes now gets this adapted look, and two things follow:

- **What stays in view fades.** An animal standing in front of a bush sees its look sink into the average. The
  *good* cells, driven by that look, fall silent, and with them the urge to bite. The animal moves on.
- **What is unusual stands out.** All berry bushes look alike in most respects, and that shared part is nearly
  always in the average. What passes through is the part that differs: the colour of *this* bush. Nothing uses
  this yet; the next stage does.

## Watching it work

One animal from the last generation, at a dud. The two `vis+0` rows are two look inputs of the eye that points
straight ahead (`vis` for vision, `+0` for its direction).

The animal walks up and bites. The dud does not change, yet what the eye reports **sinks a little with every
tick**. The *good* cells and `grasp` hold for a while, then drop out, and the biting stops. When the animal turns
away, the look inputs go *below* zero: the eye is still used to the dud and reports less of that look than usual.

<div data-life="strip" data-stage="1.2h" data-example="dud_visit"></div>

## Biology

Step into a room with a strong smell and after a few minutes it is gone. The smell is still there; the receptors
have stopped reporting it. Sensory neurons respond to *change*, and a steady input carries no news. This is
*sensory adaptation*.

*Habituation* is the same thing seen in behaviour. A snail that is touched pulls in its horns; touch it again and
again and it stops bothering. It is the simplest kind of learning, found in every animal that has been tested,
including ones with a few hundred neurons.

## The world

The world of the previous stage with one more kind of bush, the dud: it looks like a berry bush and never carries
a berry. Its colour is drawn anew for every life, so nothing an ancestor knew can tell an animal to leave it
alone. When the dud happens to have an attractive colour, an animal whose eyes do not adapt will stand at it and
bite for as long as it lives.

<div data-life="settings" data-stage="1.2h"></div>

## Did it work?

There is no group of neurons to silence here, since the change is in how the inputs work. The matching test is
to switch the adaptation off in the evolved animals and let them live again.

<div data-life="verdict" data-stage="1.2h" data-used="adaptation_off:without adaptation"></div>

**The animals rely on it heavily:** without adaptation they keep well under half their fitness. Against the old
brain the gain is smaller and uneven across seeds. The control's fitness swings from one generation to the next,
depending on whether it happens to like the colour of that generation's dud.

The clearest difference is in how a life is spent. Animals whose eyes adapt stand and bite at nothing less than
half as often:

<div data-life="bars" data-stage="1.2h" data-example="life_spent" data-rows="0,1" data-unit="%" data-col0="new brain (main)" data-col1="old brain (control)"></div>

## Full results

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Fitness over the generations"}
The first generations of main are a step back. Every inherited synapse was tuned to eyes that reported the whole
look, and the eyes now report only the difference, so the population has to re-tune before the change pays.

<div data-life="curves" data-stage="1.2h"></div>
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="What did not work: unfamiliar food"}
Without the dud, adaptation was used only a little: the long lives had already selected most of the standing
still away, and evolution can learn the look of an empty bush of every kind it has always known. Giving the good
berries a new colour in every life did not change that. What makes adaptation worth having is something that
looks like food and gives nothing, whatever colour it has.
:::
